questions.q: What does the compute-estimate formula C ≈ 6ND represent?
options: The number of GPUs needed for a training job
The total FLOPs required to train a model, where N is parameters and D is training tokens
The amount of GPU memory required
The network bandwidth required between nodes
questions.explain: C ≈ 6ND estimates total training compute in FLOPs: roughly 6 FLOPs per parameter (N) per training token (D), combining the forward pass (~2 FLOPs) and backward pass (~4 FLOPs).

questions.q: Why does the factor of 6 appear in the C ≈ 6ND formula rather than, say, 2?
options: Because there are 6 GPUs typically used per training job
Because the forward pass costs about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token, and the backward pass costs roughly twice that (4 more), totaling 6
Because each parameter is stored in 6 bytes
Because it accounts for 6 months of typical training time
questions.explain: The forward pass costs ~2 FLOPs per parameter per token; the backward pass costs about double the forward pass (~4 FLOPs), for a combined total of ~6 FLOPs per parameter per token.

questions.q: What does MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) measure, and why is it never 100% in practice?
options: The percentage of GPUs that are powered on; it's never 100% because of maintenance
The fraction of a GPU's theoretical peak FLOPs actually achieved during training; overhead from communication, data loading, and kernel launches always eats into it
The percentage of model parameters that are actively used
The fraction of training tokens that are unique
questions.explain: MFU is the realized fraction of a GPU's peak theoretical FLOPs. It's never 100% because communication overhead, data loading stalls, and other gaps always reduce effective throughput below peak.

questions.q: In the Solara-70B worked example, if the Solara ML Platform team achieved 50% MFU instead of the planned 40%, what would happen to the wall-clock training time estimate?
options: It would increase, because higher MFU means slower training
It would stay exactly the same, since MFU doesn't affect wall-clock time
It would decrease, since higher MFU means more effective FLOPs per second, requiring less wall-clock time for the same total compute
It would double
questions.explain: Wall-clock time is total compute (C) divided by effective cluster throughput (peak FLOPs × MFU × GPU count). Raising MFU increases effective throughput, which reduces the wall-clock time needed to reach the same total compute C.

questions.q: Once GPU-hours are calculated for a job, how do you convert that figure into an estimated wall-clock time?
options: Multiply GPU-hours by the number of GPUs
Divide GPU-hours by the number of GPUs running the job in parallel
GPU-hours and wall-clock time are always equal
Divide GPU-hours by the MFU percentage
questions.explain: Wall-clock time equals total GPU-hours divided by the number of GPUs running concurrently, since all GPUs work in parallel on the same job. For Solara-70B, ~413,000 GPU-hours / 512 GPUs ≈ 807 hours ≈ 33.6 days.
